answer.summary: Manik defines company-product fit as checking whether a potentially successful new product belongs in the company’s portfolio and plays to its distinctive strengths to create customer value better than competitors. Teams should assess this before product-market fit because conviction about the company-level fit helps secure understanding and sponsorship, reduce distractions, and makes the PMF search easier to pursue.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: For a new product or project at a larger company (and, he says, medium-sized companies), first ask: assuming it succeeds, does it serve the right place in the company’s product portfolio? Does it make sense for that company? Invest only when the company can play to its strengths, create unique consumer or customer value, and do so better than others. Building something merely because another company is doing it is not a good reason; if the product does not fit the portfolio, he says, do not pursue it.

sections.heading: Why consider it before product-market fit
sections.content: Company-product fit is the question before the usual “go find product-market fit” goal. If teams can answer the portfolio-fit question with conviction, the subsequent PMF search becomes easier: there are fewer distractions, people understand the effort is strategic, and it can gain appropriate sponsorship across the company. That shared understanding can also mean people step in to help if progress is difficult; it is not a guarantee of success.
